intro: 87 foods, drugs, supplements and lifestyle habits, from exercise and sleep to fasting, sauna and cold exposure, each rated on three dials: evidence, benefit and safety. Every card carries a real photo and stays collapsed until you tap it, then opens to show the mechanism, the full write-up and a link to the research behind it. Filter by category, benefit, evidence strength or mechanism in the sidebar, or just search for what you're after.
methodology: Each entry gets three dials. EVIDENCE = quality of the human data (Strong = multiple RCTs / meta-analyses; Moderate = some RCTs or consistent cohorts; Preliminary = small or early human trials; Weak = little direct human data; Mixed = conflicting). BENEFIT = likely upside for mitochondrial function specifically. SAFETY = how safe for most healthy adults. Honest caveat: human trials rarely measure mitochondria directly, so many ratings lean on the best proxies, muscle-biopsy studies, VO2max, metabolic and oxidative-stress markers, plus mechanism. This is a synthesis for orientation, not medical advice. Talk to a clinician before changing anything.

items.name: Aerobic / endurance exercise
items.summary: The single best-validated mitochondrial intervention. Muscle-biopsy RCTs and meta-analyses show endurance training raises mitochondrial content, enzyme activity and VO2max at every age.

items.name: High-intensity interval training (HIIT)
items.summary: Time-efficient and potent: trials show HIIT boosts mitochondrial content and respiration, with especially large VO2max gains. Slightly more caution for people with cardiac risk.

items.name: Resistance / strength training
items.summary: Beyond building muscle, resistance training improves mitochondrial quality and function, particularly in older adults where it partly reverses age-related decline.

items.name: Reducing sedentary time
items.summary: Breaking up prolonged sitting improves glucose handling and metabolic health; prolonged inactivity down-regulates mitochondrial genes in muscle.

items.name: Mediterranean dietary pattern
items.summary: The most robustly evidenced dietary pattern for cardiometabolic and brain health (incl. PREDIMED RCT). Rich in polyphenols and omega-3s that support mitochondrial function and lower oxidative stress.

items.name: Dietary nitrate (beetroot)
items.summary: RCTs show dietary nitrate improves mitochondrial efficiency (more ATP per oxygen) and exercise economy, one of the few foods with a direct human mitochondrial readout.

items.name: Cocoa flavanols
items.summary: Flavanols improve vascular and metabolic markers (COSMOS trial for CV events); mechanistic and small human data suggest stimulation of mitochondrial biogenesis via nitric oxide.

items.name: Coffee & caffeine
items.summary: Large cohorts link moderate coffee to lower all-cause mortality; caffeine activates AMPK and promotes autophagy/mitophagy in mechanistic studies.

items.name: Green tea (EGCG)
items.summary: Catechins activate AMPK and may support biogenesis; human data are mostly on metabolic markers and are modest.

items.name: Berries (anthocyanins)
items.summary: Anthocyanin-rich berries improve vascular and cognitive markers in small RCTs; mitochondrial effects are inferred from antioxidant and Nrf2 pathways.

items.name: Extra-virgin olive oil
items.summary: A core Mediterranean component; polyphenols like oleocanthal have anti-inflammatory and mitochondrial-protective actions, with strong cardiometabolic human evidence.

items.name: Omega-3 fatty acids (oily fish)
items.summary: EPA/DHA incorporate into mitochondrial membranes; RCTs show improved muscle mitochondrial function and metabolic markers, though outcomes vary by population.

items.name: Pomegranate / ellagitannins
items.summary: Gut bacteria convert ellagitannins to urolithin A, a mitophagy inducer with growing human trial support (see Urolithin A supplement).

items.name: Sulforaphane (broccoli sprouts)
items.summary: A potent Nrf2 activator that boosts endogenous antioxidant defenses; human trials are small but mechanistically compelling for mitochondrial protection.

items.name: Spermidine-rich foods
items.summary: Wheat germ, natto and aged cheese are spermidine sources; cohorts link higher intake to lower mortality, and small trials show autophagy induction.

items.name: Alcohol (excess)
items.summary: Chronic and heavy alcohol damages mitochondria in liver, muscle and brain, raising oxidative stress and impairing OXPHOS. No dose is clearly mitochondrially protective.

items.name: Ultra-processed foods & added sugar
items.summary: Diets high in ultra-processed food and sugar drive insulin resistance and lipotoxic mitochondrial dysfunction; strong cohort evidence links them to metabolic disease.

items.name: Creatine monohydrate
items.summary: One of the best-evidenced supplements: buffers cellular ATP via the phosphocreatine system, improving performance and possibly brain energetics. Excellent safety record.

items.name: Coenzyme Q10 / ubiquinol
items.summary: A direct electron-transport-chain carrier and antioxidant. RCTs support benefit in heart failure (Q-SYMBIO), statin myopathy and primary mitochondrial disease; general-population benefit is smaller.

items.name: Urolithin A (Mitopure)
items.summary: The rare mitophagy inducer with real human RCTs: improves muscle mitochondrial gene expression and endurance in middle-aged and older adults.

items.name: L-Carnitine / acetyl-L-carnitine
items.summary: Shuttles fatty acids into mitochondria for oxidation; RCTs show benefit in fatigue, some cardiovascular settings and carnitine-deficiency states.

items.name: Alpha-lipoic acid
items.summary: A mitochondrial enzyme cofactor and antioxidant; best human evidence is for diabetic neuropathy, with plausible broader mitochondrial support.

items.name: GlyNAC (glycine + N-acetylcysteine)
items.summary: Restores glutathione and, in small RCTs in older adults, improved mitochondrial function, insulin resistance and multiple aging markers. Promising but early.

items.name: Nicotinamide riboside (NR)
items.summary: Reliably raises blood NAD+ in humans; functional benefits (muscle, metabolic) are so far mixed and modest in RCTs. Well tolerated.

items.name: NMN (nicotinamide mononucleotide)
items.summary: Another NAD+ precursor with early human trials suggesting improved muscle insulin sensitivity and physical measures; evidence is still thin and regulatory status is in flux.

items.name: PQQ (pyrroloquinoline quinone)
items.summary: Small human trials suggest PQQ influences mitochondrial biogenesis markers and fatigue; evidence is limited and short-term.

items.name: Riboflavin (B2) & niacin (B3)
items.summary: Cofactors for the respiratory chain; riboflavin helps specific riboflavin-responsive mitochondrial disorders, and niacin raised NAD+ and muscle strength in a small mitochondrial-myopathy trial.

items.name: Magnesium
items.summary: ATP is biologically active as Mg-ATP; deficiency impairs energy metabolism, and correcting low magnesium improves metabolic and muscular function.

items.name: Vitamin D (if deficient)
items.summary: Correcting deficiency improved muscle mitochondrial oxidative function in human studies; benefit in already-replete people is unclear.

items.name: Melatonin
items.summary: Concentrates in mitochondria as a potent antioxidant and supports circadian alignment; human mitochondrial-outcome data are early but mechanistically strong.

items.name: MitoQ (mito-targeted CoQ)
items.summary: A CoQ derivative engineered to accumulate inside mitochondria; small human trials show vascular improvements, but broad clinical benefit is unproven.

items.name: Resveratrol
items.summary: A famous SIRT1/PGC-1α activator on paper, but human trials are inconsistent and often null; may even blunt some exercise adaptations. Underwhelming so far.

items.name: Curcumin
items.summary: Anti-inflammatory and Nrf2-activating; human evidence is limited by poor bioavailability, though formulated versions show modest metabolic effects.

items.name: Taurine
items.summary: Essential for mitochondrial tRNA function; a 2023 aging paper generated buzz, but strong human longevity or mitochondrial-outcome RCTs are still lacking.

items.name: Metformin
items.summary: Mildly inhibits Complex I and activates AMPK, a hormetic stress that improves metabolic health; the TAME trial is testing aging endpoints. Note it can blunt some exercise gains.

items.name: SGLT2 inhibitors
items.summary: Prescription diabetes/heart-failure drugs that shift fuel use toward ketones and appear to improve mitochondrial and cardiac energetics; mitochondrial-specific human data are emerging.

items.name: GLP-1 receptor agonists
items.summary: By improving weight and glycemic control, GLP-1 drugs relieve metabolic stress on mitochondria; direct mitochondrial human evidence is indirect and early.

items.name: Rapamycin (off-label)
items.summary: Inhibits mTOR to boost autophagy and mitochondrial quality control, powerful in animal lifespan studies, but human anti-aging evidence is preliminary and it carries real immune/metabolic risks.

items.name: Statins
items.summary: Cardioprotective overall, but they lower CoQ10 and can impair muscle mitochondrial function in susceptible people (statin-associated myopathy). A genuine double-edged case for mitochondria.

items.name: Berberine
items.summary: A plant alkaloid (sold OTC) that activates AMPK much like metformin, with meta-analyses supporting glycemic and lipid benefits; direct mitochondrial human data are limited.

items.name: Time-restricted eating (TRE)
items.summary: Confining eating to a window improves metabolic markers in RCTs; the mitophagy/biogenesis mechanisms are strong in animals and emerging in humans.

items.name: Intermittent fasting (ADF / 5:2)
items.summary: Alternate-day and 5:2 fasting produce weight loss and metabolic benefits comparable to calorie restriction; mitochondrial adaptations are inferred from metabolic switching.

items.name: Caloric restriction
items.summary: The CALERIE RCT showed sustained moderate calorie restriction increased muscle mitochondrial biogenesis markers and reduced oxidative damage in healthy adults.

items.name: Fasting-mimicking diet (FMD)
items.summary: Periodic low-calorie 'fasting-mimicking' cycles improved metabolic and aging biomarkers in human trials; longer-term and mitochondrial-specific data are still building.

items.name: Ketogenic diet
items.summary: Well-established for epilepsy (a mitochondrially-mediated effect) and promising for metabolic conditions; ketones may boost mitochondrial biogenesis, but adherence, lipids and long-term safety warrant caution.

items.name: Exogenous ketones / MCT oil
items.summary: Ketone esters and medium-chain triglycerides raise blood ketones as an efficient mitochondrial fuel; human functional benefits are early and context-dependent.

items.name: Adequate sleep (7–9 h)
items.summary: Sleep is when much mitochondrial and metabolic housekeeping happens; observational and experimental data tie short sleep to impaired mitochondrial and metabolic function.

items.name: Treating sleep apnea (CPAP)
items.summary: Obstructive sleep apnea causes intermittent hypoxia that damages mitochondria and raises oxidative stress; CPAP reverses much of the metabolic and oxidative burden.

items.name: Chronic sleep deprivation
items.summary: Curtailed or fragmented sleep raises oxidative stress and impairs insulin sensitivity and mitochondrial function, a common, modifiable mitochondrial stressor.

items.name: Mindfulness meditation
items.summary: Mindfulness-based programs lower stress and inflammatory markers in RCTs; mitochondrial links run through reduced 'mitochondrial allostatic load' from chronic stress.

items.name: Chronic psychological stress
items.summary: Sustained stress and glucocorticoids alter mitochondrial structure and function ('mitochondrial allostatic load'), a well-argued pathway from psychology to cellular energetics.

items.name: Yoga & breathwork
items.summary: Yoga and slow-breathing practices improve HRV and stress/oxidative markers in trials; direct mitochondrial readouts are limited but the stress-reduction pathway is plausible.

items.name: Circadian alignment
items.summary: The circadian clock directly schedules mitochondrial biogenesis, dynamics and mitophagy; keeping regular light, meal and sleep timing supports that rhythm. Shift work disrupts it.

items.name: Morning bright-light exposure
items.summary: Morning outdoor light anchors the circadian clock and improves sleep and mood in trials; mitochondrial benefit is indirect, via better circadian and metabolic regulation.

items.name: Circadian disruption / shift work
items.summary: Night-shift and irregular light-dark exposure desynchronize mitochondrial and metabolic rhythms and are linked in cohorts to metabolic and cardiovascular disease.

items.name: Red / near-infrared light (photobiomodulation)
items.summary: Red/NIR light is absorbed by Complex IV (cytochrome c oxidase), transiently boosting ATP output. Small human trials show muscle-recovery and some cognitive effects; protocols vary widely.

items.name: Sauna bathing
items.summary: Finnish cohorts strongly link frequent sauna to lower cardiovascular and all-cause mortality; heat stress induces heat-shock proteins and may drive mitochondrial biogenesis (heat as exercise-mimetic).

items.name: Hot-water immersion / passive heat
items.summary: Repeated hot baths improve vascular function and glycemic control in small trials, with heat-shock-protein pathways implicated in mitochondrial adaptation.

items.name: Cold exposure / cold-water immersion
items.summary: Cold activates brown/beige fat and PGC-1α-driven mitochondrial biogenesis in humans; benefits for metabolism are real but modest, and cold right after strength training can blunt gains.

items.name: Whole-body cryotherapy
items.summary: Popular for recovery, but controlled evidence for lasting mitochondrial or performance benefit is weak and inconsistent compared with simple cold-water immersion.

items.name: Strong social connection
items.summary: Robust cohort evidence ties social connection to longevity; the mitochondrial link is indirect, via lower chronic stress, inflammation and better health behaviours.

items.name: Loneliness / social isolation
items.summary: Chronic loneliness raises inflammatory and stress signalling and predicts worse health outcomes in large cohorts, a plausible upstream driver of mitochondrial stress.

items.name: Cognitive training / mental engagement
items.summary: Mentally demanding activity engages neuronal energy metabolism and supports cognitive reserve, but direct evidence that 'brain training' improves mitochondrial function is minimal. Included for completeness and honesty.

items.name: Air pollution (PM2.5)
items.summary: Fine-particulate exposure is associated in human biomarker studies with mitochondrial DNA damage, altered mtDNA copy number and oxidative stress. Reducing exposure matters.

items.name: Tobacco smoking
items.summary: Smoking directly damages the respiratory chain and mitochondrial DNA and is one of the most robustly harmful mitochondrial exposures known. Quitting is the highest-impact fix here.

items.name: Heavy metals & pesticides
items.summary: Many environmental toxicants (arsenic, lead, certain pesticides like rotenone/paraquat) inhibit respiratory complexes and are linked to mitochondrial disease and Parkinson's risk.

items.name: Green space & nature exposure
items.summary: Access to green space is linked in cohorts to lower stress and better cardiometabolic health; the mitochondrial benefit is indirect, through stress reduction and more physical activity.

items.name: Cardiorespiratory fitness (VO₂max)
items.summary: Your VO₂max is essentially a whole-body readout of mitochondrial oxidative capacity, and one of the strongest predictors of all-cause mortality in large cohorts. Raising it is the headline goal of most training.

items.name: Nuts
items.summary: Regular nut intake is tied in large cohorts and trials to lower cardiometabolic risk and mortality; their polyphenols and unsaturated fats support membranes and lower oxidative stress.

items.name: Dietary fibre & fermented foods
items.summary: Gut bacteria ferment fibre into short-chain fatty acids like butyrate, the primary fuel for colon-cell mitochondria, and higher intake improves metabolic and inflammatory markers.

items.name: Legumes & plant protein
items.summary: A Blue-Zones staple: swapping some animal protein for legumes is associated with better metabolic profiles and longevity, easing the metabolic load on mitochondria.

items.name: Chronic overeating (positive energy balance)
items.summary: Persistent calorie surplus floods mitochondria with more fuel than they can cleanly burn, driving reactive-oxygen production and insulin resistance, arguably the most common mitochondrial stressor of all.

items.name: Astaxanthin
items.summary: A carotenoid that sits inside membranes as an unusually potent antioxidant; small human trials suggest benefits for muscle endurance and skin, with mitochondrial protection as the proposed mechanism.

items.name: Selenium
items.summary: An essential cofactor for glutathione peroxidase, a key mitochondrial antioxidant enzyme; correcting deficiency helps, but excess selenium is toxic, dose matters.

items.name: Vitamin E (tocopherols)
items.summary: A fat-soluble membrane antioxidant in theory, but large trials are mostly null and high doses have shown harm signals. Underwhelming as a supplement despite the tidy mechanism.

items.name: Methylene blue (low-dose)
items.summary: At low doses it can shuttle electrons to Complex IV, potentially rescuing stalled respiration; small human cognition studies are intriguing, but it interacts dangerously with serotonergic drugs.

items.name: Citrulline / L-arginine
items.summary: These amino acids raise nitric oxide, a signal for mitochondrial biogenesis and better blood flow; ergogenic trials are mixed but the vascular/mito rationale is sound.

items.name: D-ribose
items.summary: A sugar that feeds directly into ATP regeneration; small trials in heart failure and fatigue syndromes are suggestive but far from conclusive.

items.name: Quercetin
items.summary: A polyphenol studied for mitochondrial biogenesis and (with dasatinib) as a senolytic; human mitochondrial-outcome data are thin and effects modest.

items.name: Pioglitazone
items.summary: A prescription diabetes drug that activates PPARγ to promote mitochondrial biogenesis and insulin sensitivity, but carries weight-gain, fluid-retention and fracture risks.

items.name: Consistent sleep timing
items.summary: Sleep *regularity*, going to bed and waking at steady times, predicts metabolic health and mortality independent of duration, keeping the clock that schedules mitochondrial housekeeping on track.

items.name: Sunlight for vitamin D
items.summary: Sensible sun exposure drives natural vitamin D synthesis, linked to muscle mitochondrial function, balanced against real skin-cancer risk, so moderation and skin type matter.

items.name: Avoiding bright light at night
items.summary: Evening light, especially blue, suppresses melatonin and desynchronises the circadian clock; dimming screens and lights at night helps protect the rhythms that govern mitochondrial repair.

items.name: A sense of purpose
items.summary: A strong sense of purpose predicts lower mortality and inflammation in large cohorts; the mitochondrial link is indirect, via reduced chronic-stress signalling.

items.name: Microplastics & plasticizers
items.summary: A fast-moving concern: micro- and nanoplastics and plasticizers (like phthalates) show mitochondrial and endocrine-disrupting effects in lab and early biomarker studies. Reducing exposure is prudent.

items.name: Novelty & lifelong learning
items.summary: Learning new, demanding skills engages neuronal energy metabolism and builds cognitive reserve; direct evidence that it improves mitochondrial function is minimal, included for honesty.

items.name: Contrast (hot–cold) therapy
items.summary: Alternating heat and cold is popular for recovery and circulation; controlled evidence for a lasting mitochondrial benefit beyond the sum of sauna and cold is limited and mixed.
